# Whatever Comes

When someone says *write whatever comes to you*, what comes, at first, is not a subject. It's static. A list with no theme: the smell of a school gymnasium, floor wax and rubber and echo. A drum fill from a song I could hum but not name. The plot of a movie I've watched three times and could not summarize under oath. A phone number that belonged to a house we don't live in anymore. Whether the stove is off. The thing I meant to say to someone I no longer see. A single birthday candle, still in its wrapper. A key to a lock we no longer own. The instructions for a bookshelf we gave away years ago, kept in a drawer for no reason at all.

The mind, offered total freedom, behaves like a junk drawer flung open. Everything in there is true. Nothing in there is a topic.

So the job is not invention. The job is choosing. Writing, I've come to believe, is mostly the nerve to reach into the drawer, pick up one thing, and say: this. This was the point all along. You have to say it like you mean it, because the meaning arrives later, on the page, if you're lucky.

Okay. Reaching in. Eyes closed. Here.

Chlorine.

That's what came. Not a story, not a person: just the smell, sudden and green and sharp, catching in the throat at the edge of a public pool. Fine. Follow it down.

I was seven, maybe eight, the age of municipal swimming lessons, when fear of water is still official and therefore treatable. Every Tuesday my mother walked me to the pool and left me at the gate. The locker room smelled of mildew and lost things. The water got me at the ankles first, cold as a rumor, and I went in the rest of the way by degrees, the way you slide into sleep. Our instructor was a wide, calm woman who stood in the shallow end as though the pool were her kitchen. Mrs. Delgado. She was unimpressed by all of it: the flailing, the gulped mouthfuls, the drama. She had watched a thousand children discover they couldn't breathe underwater, and none of it had ever struck her as remarkable. Somewhere behind her, a man with a net fed chemicals into the water. The pool's quiet pharmacist.

The day I remember is floating day. "I'll put my hands under your back," Mrs. Delgado said. "Lean back. Let your head go." But the head is the problem, isn't it? The head is where the fearing happens. I leaned back exactly none of the way. My fingers made claws of the air. Water lapped at my ears like it wanted to tell me something.

"You're trying to float," she said, in the voice of a woman stating the weather. "You can't try to float. Stop trying."

Which sounds like a riddle until, for one half-second, you actually do it. My head went back. My ears went under and the whole world changed frequency, shouts becoming ocean, the lifeguard's whistle becoming a gull, tiles becoming sky, and I was held. Not by effort. By water. The ceiling lights wavered overhead like something seen from very far away. I had been buoyant the entire time. The only thing that had ever threatened to sink me was my own thrashing.

Afterward she took her hands away without telling me, and I stayed up anyway. The hands had been a ceremony. I floated alone with my eyes wide open, like a person discovering they had been rich all along.

I think about that every time I face a blank page, and never more than now, holding a thousand words and no instructions. Because the temptation of total freedom is to thrash. Somewhere out there is the impressive topic, a war, a moon landing, an elegy, and I hunt for it the way you pat your pockets for keys you're already holding. But freedom has no right answer. Freedom is the deep end. You cannot try your way to the true subject any more than you can try your way to floating. You stop. You lie back. You give the page your weight.

And it isn't only pages. It's an empty Saturday, a new city, the first week of grief, the first week of anything. Whatever is completely open defeats the performer in you, because performance needs a rubric and an audience, and freedom supplies neither. All freedom supplies is water.

We pretend we want no limits, but hand a person a blank eternity and watch them freeze. Give the same person seventeen syllables and they'll hand you back a haiku by lunch. The sonnet has fourteen lines and a rhyme scheme, and it has outlived every empire that ever mocked it. This is not really a paradox. The limits are Mrs. Delgado's hands. Even this prompt, generous as it is, has a shape: a thousand words is a vessel, and edges are what let you relax inside it.

The thousand words are running out now. I can hear them going, the way you hear a wave leave the shore. I don't mind. Because this is what came, and it turns out the smell of chlorine was holding a whole summer inside it, and the summer was holding the lesson, and the lesson is this: whatever comes, when it finally comes, will not be what you were hunting for. It will be smaller and stranger and greener, and it will have been waiting in the drawer the whole time, patient as a key. You don't grab it. You lie back. It holds you.

No one floats to shore. But you can float all the way to the far edge, to the last word, where the tiles are, and put your feet down, and stand: dripping, unimpressed with yourself, lighter than when you went in.

The prompt is completely open: "You have 1000 words. Write whatever comes to you." This is an invitation to write freely — no constraints on genre, subject, or form. The interesting thing here is what "whatever comes to you" means. It's almost a Rorschach test. Some people would write fiction, some poetry, some an essay about the prompt itself.

I have a few options:
1. Write a short story
2. Write a personal essay / reflective piece
3. Write something meta about the prompt itself
4. Write poetry
5. Write something experimental that plays with the constraint

What would be genuinely good here? The prompt is playful and open. A purely meta response ("Well, when given freedom, I find it hard to choose...") risks being self-indulgent and clichéd. But a straight short story ignores the interesting frame of the prompt.

I think the best move is something that feels alive — writing that acknowledges the strange freedom of the prompt without being navel-gazing about it. Maybe a piece that starts with the blank page situation and spirals into something. Or a piece of fiction that has emotional weight.

Actually, let me think about what would delight a reader. If I were reading a response to this prompt, what would I want? I'd want something that feels like it could only have been written *in this moment*, something with voice, something surprising. Not a safe short story about, like, a lighthouse keeper (though honestly those can be great).

Let me consider a few directions:

Direction A: An essay about choice and constraint — the paradox that being given 1000 words and total freedom is paralyzing. This is honest and could be genuinely interesting if done well, exploring how constraint enables creativity. It could weave in examples: sonnets, haiku, Oulipo, Dr. Seuss with "Green Eggs and Ham." Then it could turn — the writer realizes that the answer to freedom is to simply begin, and the piece becomes something. There's a nice recursive quality.

Direction B: A short story that begins mid-thought, feeling like something written spontaneously. Something about ordinary life made strange.

Direction C: A hybrid — start meta, pivot into a vignette, come back out. This mirrors how actual thought works when you're given an open prompt: you orbit, you land somewhere unexpected.

I like Direction C, or a version of Direction A that ends by actually writing something. Let me draft mentally.

The honest truth of "write whatever comes to you" is that what comes first is noise: the checkout line, a half-remembered song, the smell of rain, worry about something, a face. The mind doesn't generate "content" — it generates fragments. A good piece could dramatize that: the first thing that comes to you is never a subject, it's a sensation. And then the act of writing is the act of choosing one fragment and following it down.

So maybe: the piece begins by admitting the mind is a hallway of doors, all ajar. Then it picks one door — a memory, an image — and walks through it. The middle becomes a small, specific thing: a description of, say, my father teaching me to skip stones, or a woman on a bus, or the last day of a house being emptied. Something concrete and felt. Then it returns to the frame at the end: this is what I chose; the other doors are still ajar; somewhere in you, reader, they are too.

Wait — should I write as an AI? Should the piece acknowledge that I'm an AI deciding what to write? That could be interesting and honest, but it risks centering the AI-ness when the human asked for writing, not a statement about my nature. I think a light touch: I can write in first person without making a big deal of whether the "I" is "real." Actually, fiction and essay blur here. The prompt says "whatever comes to you" — so the piece can be about what comes, generically human or specifically mine, and the ambiguity is fine. Most readers of this prompt want to read something good, not a meditation on my ontology. I'll write in a first person that's human-flavored but not claiming false specific autobiographical facts presented as literal truth — or, honestly, in a creative prompt context, inventing a speaker is standard practice. A lyrical essay with an invented "I" is fine. But I could also keep it more universal: "you," "one," "we." Hmm. First person is warmer.

Let me think about the fragment at the center. What's a rich, specific image? Options:
- Skipping stones with a father
- A grocery store at 2 a.m.
- Someone learning their grandmother's recipe after she's gone
- Moving out of an apartment
- A snow day
- Watching someone sleep on a train
- The sound of a screen door

The screen door is nice and small. Or the stone-skipping. Or — here's a thought — the piece could center on the idea of "whatever comes first": what actually comes first to a mind is rarely grand. It's the smell of chlorine. The specific green of a pool. Chlorine is a good trigger-smell, universally loaded with summer.

Alternatively, the central vignette could be about a word itself — like the word "petrichor" or the way a certain phrase sticks. Hmm, that might be too cute.

Let me try to actually sketch the piece:

Opening: When someone says "write whatever comes," what comes is not a subject but static. Inventory of the static: a half-remembered phone number, the drum solo from a song, the blue light of a fish tank, the exact anxiety of an unanswered email. The mind as a junk drawer. Then: writing is choosing one thing from the drawer and pretending it was always the point.

Turn: Okay. Here's one thing. Then the vignette.

Vignette idea — the fish tank. A waiting room with a fish tank? Or the pool. Let me go with the pool: summers, chlorine, the specific terror and joy of the deep end, a swimming instructor, the moment of learning to float. Floating is a nice metaphor for this very exercise: you can't float by trying hard; you have to give in, trust the water. That maps beautifully onto the prompt: given total freedom, you can't strain; you have to relax into it and be held. The essay can land on that: whatever comes to you comes when you stop demanding it come. Floating as the answer to the blank page. That's a genuine insight, not just a conceit — writing teachers really do say this, and it's true of the prompt.

1. The static/junk drawer of first thoughts (150-200 words). Playful, list-like, honest.
2. The pivot: choosing one item — chlorine (200 words): why this one? Because it came first, or because it's the one that opened? But the impressive thing is never the intended thing; it's the true one. Constraint paradox: sonnet, haiku — forms set you free. Voice: conversational but precise. First person. Some short sentences. The mind, offered total freedom, behaves like a junk drawer flung open. Everything in there is true. Nothing in there is a topic.

So the job is not invention. The job is choosing. Writing, I've come to think, is mostly the nerve to reach into the drawer, pick up one thing, and say: this. This was the point all along. You have to say it like you believe it, because the believing arrives later, on the page, if you're lucky.

I was seven, maybe eight, the age of municipal swimming lessons, when fear of water is still official and therefore treatable. Every Tuesday my mother walked me to the pool, and every Tuesday the water got me at the ankles first, cold as a rumor, before I eased in the rest of the way like a letter being opened. The instructor was a wide, calm woman who stood in the shallow end as if the pool were her kitchen. Her name was Mrs. Delgado, and she was unimpressed by all of it — our flailing, our gulped mouthfuls, our drama. She had seen a thousand children discover that they could not breathe underwater, and she found us none of it remarkable.

The day I remember is floating day. "I'll put my hands under your back," she said. "Lean back. Let your head go." But the head is the problem, isn't it? The head is where the fearing happens. I leaned back exactly none of the way. My fingers made claws of the air. Water lapped at my ears like it wanted to tell me something.

"You're trying to float," Mrs. Delgado said, in the voice of a woman stating the weather. "You can't try to float. Stop trying."

Which is the kind of advice that sounds like a riddle until, for one half-second, you actually do it. My head went back. My ears went under, and the whole world changed frequency — shouts becoming ocean, tiles becoming sky. And I was held. Not by effort. By water. The ceiling lights wavered above me like something seen from very far away. I had been buoyant the entire time. The only thing that had ever threatened to sink me was my own thrashing.

I think about this every time I face a blank page, and never more than now, holding a thousand words and no instructions. Because the temptation of total freedom is to thrash. Somewhere there is an impressive topic — a war, a theorem, a elegy — wait, "a elegy" typo — "an elegy." Somewhere there is a subject that would make me sound serious, and I can feel myself hunting for it the way you pat your pockets for keys you're already holding. But freedom has no right answer. Freedom is the deep end. You can't try your way to the true subject any more than you can try your way to floating. You stop. You lie back. You give the page your weight.

We pretend we want no limits, but hand a person a blank eternity and watch them freeze. Give the same person seventeen syllables and they'll build you a haiku by lunch. The sonnet has fourteen lines and a rhyme scheme, and it has outlived every empire that mocked it. This is not a paradox, really. The limits are Mrs. Delgado's hands. Even this prompt, generous as it is, has a shape — a thousand words is a vessel, and the edges are what let you relax inside it.

The thousand words are running out now. I can hear them going, the way you hear a wave leaving. And I don't mind. Because this is what came, and it turns out the smell of chlorine was holding a whole summer inside it, and the summer was holding the lesson, and the lesson is this: whatever comes, when it finally comes, will not be what you were hunting for. It will be smaller and stranger and greener, and it will have been waiting in the drawer the whole time, patient as a key. You don't grab it. You lie back. It holds you.

No one floats to shore. But you can float all the way to the far edge of the pool, to the last word, where the tiles are, and put your feet down, and stand — dripping, unimpressive, lighter than you went in.
